references.text: Israel's elders came to Samuel and asked for a king 'like all the nations', directly fulfilling the warning prophecy in Deuteronomy that the people would desire a king like their neighboring peoples.
The people refused to listen to Samuel and said they wanted a king 'like all other nations', reflecting the wording of Deuteronomy 17:14.
Samuel rebukes the people for rejecting God by asking for a king, showing that the demand for a king was a spiritual failure that Moses had foreseen.
Samuel reminds the people that they asked for a king when they saw the enemy approaching, even though the Lord was their king. This connects to their desire to be like other nations.
Moses warns that the Lord will lead the people and their king to a nation they do not know, presupposing that Israel would have a king as described in 17:14.
God's promise to Abraham that the land would be given to his descendants is the background for the expression 'the land that the Lord your God gives you'.
The description of crossing the Jordan and living securely in the land parallels Deuteronomy 17:14's description of taking possession of the land and dwelling there.
